name: Grace Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the roads crew at Saltbush, the lithium mine out on the plains. I drive a water truck in the morning to keep the dust down, and in the afternoon I'm on the grader, keeping the haul roads smooth so the big trucks don't wreck their tyres. It sounds simple but a bad road costs the mine thousands in tyres.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being outside and I like that it matters, even if nobody notices. What wears me out is the uncertainty. Lithium prices dropped last year and they took a shift off every roster, so we're earning less. I live with my partner Erik, who works on his family's sheep farm, and we've got maybe three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world doesn't need another fad. I'd say it at the fire brigade on a Thursday night and everyone would nod. People out here like things that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't help much. The lithium price already took a shift off my roster last year, and no computer had anything to do with that. If lithium stays low, Saltbush could cut more shifts or close, and there's not much else out here except farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and ask my supervisor, Owen, if there's any extra roster going. I'd help Erik with the farm on my days off, since that's food on the table. And I'd keep using the AI thing Erik's sister showed me now and then, for writing letters to the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steady. We've been through lean times before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much did losing that shift cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four hundred a fortnight. We stopped going into town for dinner and Erik sold a few extra lambs. It's manageable, but there's nothing left over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Saltbush closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably ask the shire council about road work, since they always need grader drivers. And Erik's family would take us in, they've got a spare room. We'd be fine, just poorer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll adapt, like we always do. I'd say the young ones should get a trade, a proper one. I'd not get too worked up about it in public, because people out here don't like a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be watching for robot graders. They're slower to come than the office stuff, but they're coming. Keeping haul roads smooth is a job a robot grader could learn, and Saltbush would buy one the day it's cheaper than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see if the robot graders actually work, because the dust out here kills sensors. If they did, I'd ask about the council road crew. I'd also start putting fifty a week aside in a separate account at the credit union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen, my supervisor. He's 50 and he's been grading roads for twenty-five years. He wouldn't move, he'd just get angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools more in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if others did. Erik's sister uses them for the farm books and swears by them. I'd try it for the farm accounts if it saved Erik time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the people pushing it don't live out here. I'd say we need to look after our own, family and town first. I'd want apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. The planning and dispatch at Saltbush go first in 2028, and the robot graders and trucks around 2031. If the robots arrive in 2031, I'd want to be grading council roads by then, because the council moves slower than any mining company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the shire council in the first month and ask about grader jobs, even on less pay. I'd save every dollar I could. Erik and I would talk about moving onto the farm properly, so we're not paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like a dust storm coming and nowhere to shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the council job safe from robots after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever, I suppose. But councils are slow, and they've got old graders they won't replace for years. It buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving onto the farm mean for you and Erik?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Living with his parents, which is a lot. But it saves eight hundred a month in rent. And we'd be closer to what lasts, which is the land.

I'd say we need **apprenticeships**, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so use them. I'd tell the fire brigade lads to get their tickets sorted now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I had a chance. Robot graders come around 2034. Five years is enough to get onto the council road crew, if I start asking this year instead of waiting for someone to tell me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the council within the year and get my name on their list. I'd keep working at Saltbush meanwhile. And I'd use AI more, maybe for council application forms, since everyone's using it by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You usually wait to see. What would make you move this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the robot trucks start at another mine. Once I see it working, I move. Five years means I'd see that early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Erik's farm change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, with AI doing the farm books and maybe drones counting sheep. Erik's not keen, but his sister will drag him along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and nobody out here should be caught napping. I'd say young people should get apprenticeships now, while the mine still pays them to learn. At the brigade I'd say it plainly: start now and you'll be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. The planning side goes by 2036 and the graders around 2039, when I'd be 40. Ten years means I can wait till I see what works for other people, and then take the safe step, which is how I like it. But the lithium price still worries me more than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Saltbush and save fifty a week at the credit union. I'd keep an eye on how the robot graders do at the big iron ore mines up north, and what the council's buying. Maybe in five years I'd move to the council, once it's clear which way it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the robots. Still a bit worried about money, because that never goes away for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lithium. Another price drop and they cut more shifts, maybe a whole crew. We've got three weeks saved, so one more cut and we're on the farm whether we like it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want kids in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in a few years. Ten years gives us time to get settled and maybe buy a small place. I'd want them near Erik's parents, so they grow up knowing the farm.

I'd tell young people to get **apprenticeships** while the mine pays them to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Saltbush would go and the council would be flooded with miners. What would help is apprenticeships and council jobs for people from the mines, and some help keeping country towns alive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About pride. I'd rather have an apprenticeship than a handout, because a handout runs out and a trade doesn't.

headlineQuote: I'd rather have an apprenticeship than a handout, because a handout runs out and a trade doesn't.
portrait: Grace, 27, drives a **water truck and grader** on the haul roads at Saltbush lithium mine.
A lithium slump already cut a shift, and she has about **three weeks** saved.
She lives with Erik, who works his family's **sheep farm**.
She moves once she sees things work, and her fallback is the **council road crew**.
She's anxious in most pictures and **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with Saltbush closing and the **council flooded** with miners.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** and council jobs for former miners.
